wizened

/WIZ-uhnd/ - the stress falls on WIZ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Wizened means dry, shrunken, wrinkled.

The bristlecone's wizened trunk, two thousand years of wind-carved knots, is barely wider than a fence post.

Example

Appalachian apple dolls get their wizened faces from the fruit itself: carved fresh, then left to dry for a month until the cheeks pucker into an old woman's smile — the shrinking does the sculpting.

Wizened is the precise word because it names all three changes at once — dried out, shrunken, and creased. Wrinkled alone could describe damp laundry; wizened tells you moisture left slowly and took size with it, the signature of long age.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

shriveled: Shriveled means shrunken and wrinkled from lost moisture, and it is age-neutral — a balloon, a grape, or yesterday's peeled orange can shrivel in a day. Wizened adds the signature of long time: slow drying that leaves hands, faces, and orchard apples creased. Anything can be shriveled; only the aged look wizened.

gnarled: Gnarled means knotted and twisted, like old wood or arthritic knuckles — the shape itself has warped. Wizened is about drying and shrinking: moisture gone, surface creased, size reduced. An oak root can be gnarled yet full of sap; a wizened apple twists nowhere but shrinks and creases.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

plump: full and rounded with moisture

smooth: unlined, with no creases at all

Where it sits · how far the shriveling has gone

dried → wizened → mummified

dried vs. wizened: Dried has simply lost its moisture — it stops short of wizened, which has shrunk and creased along the way.

mummified vs. wizened: Mummified goes further than wizened: nothing is left but a preserved husk.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — wizen: to dry up, to shrivel (Old English wisnian)

Suffix — -ed: past participle: having undergone it

Put it together: Wizen (to dry up) + -ed (having undergone it) = having dried and shriveled. Old English wisnian described withering crops a thousand years ago; the verb itself nearly vanished, but its participle stayed behind to describe faces, hands, and apples that time has dried into folds.

Why there's no relative to spot: The old verb wizen survives only inside this participle — nobody today says a plum 'wizens' on the counter, and the root built no other English words. One caution while you're here: wizened has nothing to do with wise or wizard; the resemblance is pure coincidence.

Strength Check

Word Choice

neutral / vivid

Wizened is for living things and once-plump produce — elders, hands, apples, roots — dried and creased by time. Shriveled is the plainer, age-neutral word; gnarled adds twisting, as in old wood. And resist the sound-alike trap: wizened means dried by age, not made wise by it.
